movements.name: Taller de Gráfica Popular
movements.summary: A Mexico City print collective that made the linocut and woodcut a cheap, fast, collective broadside medium for labour, anti-fascist and revolutionary causes.

principles.name: The cheapest block wins
principles.idea: Linoleum and wood blocks cut fast and print on any paper, so a message could go from meeting to wall in days without a commercial printer.
principles.example: TGP broadsides and handbills of the Cárdenas years, from 1937

principles.name: Collective authorship
principles.idea: Work was often made collaboratively and editions were deliberately left unnumbered, refusing the collectible-print economy.
principles.example: TGP portfolios sold under the La Estampa Mexicana imprint

principles.name: The vernacular as the source
principles.idea: The popular broadside and the calavera of José Guadalupe Posada and Manuel Manilla, not academic art, set the visual language.
principles.example: TGP's revival of the satirical calavera, 1940s

principles.name: Narrative in black and white
principles.idea: Dense gouged blacks, figures massed in crowds and a single strong diagonal tell a political story in one image without colour.
principles.example: Leopoldo Méndez, En el nombre de Cristo, lithographs, 1942

keyWorks.title: En el nombre de Cristo (series of seven lithographs)
Illustrations for Juan de la Cabada, Incidentes melódicos del mundo irracional

movements.name: Argentine Modernism
movements.summary: From the 1945 Arte Concreto-Invención group to the Di Tella design department and the 1971-72 Buenos Aires signage plan: invention, then system.

principles.name: Invent, don't represent
principles.idea: The invencionistas rejected illusion and symbolism: a work is a concrete object of colour, plane and line, not a picture of something else.
principles.example: Manifiesto Invencionista, Buenos Aires, 1946

principles.name: Theory travels in print
principles.idea: A small magazine can carry a whole design culture across a continent by publishing art, architecture, industrial design and typography side by side.
principles.example: Nueva Visión, edited by Tomás Maldonado and Alfredo Hlito, 1951-1957

principles.name: One house, one voice
principles.idea: An institution's posters, catalogues and programmes share a single visual identity produced by an in-house department, mixing Swiss order with New York wit.
principles.example: Departamento de Diseño Gráfico, Instituto Di Tella, formalised 1963 under Juan Carlos Distéfano

principles.name: Design the street
principles.idea: A city's signs, street names and public information are one coherent system, designed as public infrastructure rather than as individual objects.
principles.example: González Ruiz and Shakespear, Plan Visual de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, 1971-1972

keyWorks.title: Instituto Di Tella graphic identity and posters
Plan Visual de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires

movements.name: Brazilian Concretism
movements.summary: Concrete painting, the Noigandres poets and Ulm-trained designers turned Brazil's industrial boom into a geometric, word-as-object visual culture and a national identity practice.

principles.name: The word is a thing
principles.idea: A poem is a visual-verbal object built from the space of the page; syntax is replaced by spatial arrangement, so typography carries the meaning.
principles.example: Augusto de Campos, Haroldo de Campos and Décio Pignatari, Plano-piloto para poesia concreta, Noigandres 4, 1958

principles.name: Art meets industry
principles.idea: Geometric art is not decoration but a method for industrial society; the same artists founded design offices and furniture factories.
principles.example: Geraldo de Barros, Unilabor furniture cooperative, São Paulo, from 1954

principles.name: The sign without the name
principles.idea: Identity is carried by a simple, constructed symbol strong enough that the company name can be dropped.
principles.example: Forminform, Sardinhas Coqueiro mark built from semicircles, 1958

principles.name: Teach it as a discipline
principles.idea: Design becomes a university subject on the Ulm model, with method, theory and industry links, not a branch of fine art.
principles.example: Escola Superior de Desenho Industrial (ESDI), Rio de Janeiro, opened 1963

principles.name: The nation as client
principles.idea: Modernist identity is applied to the state itself: anniversaries, broadcasters and the currency.
principles.example: Aloísio Magalhães, winning cruzeiro novo banknote design competition, 1966

keyWorks.title: Poster for the first Bienal de São Paulo (Antonio Maluf)
IV Centenário do Rio de Janeiro symbol

movements.name: Venezuelan Modernism
movements.summary: Oil-funded Caracas, where émigré designers and kinetic artists made corporate magazines, museum catalogues and alphabets into experiments in perception and print.

principles.name: The magazine as laboratory
principles.idea: A corporate house magazine, freed from selling, becomes a place to test paper, folds, screens and typographic structure issue by issue.
principles.example: El Farol (Creole Petroleum), art-directed by Gerd Leufert 1957-1959 and Nedo 1959-1972

principles.name: Exhibit the discipline
principles.idea: Showing design in a museum establishes it as a culture in its own right, not a by-product of advertising.
principles.example: Gráfica 1, Museo de Bellas Artes, Caracas, 1961, the country's first graphic design exhibition

principles.name: Perception as material
principles.idea: Colour and line are treated as events that change with the viewer's movement, not as fixed fills.
principles.example: Carlos Cruz-Diez, first Physichromie, 1959

principles.name: Letters as impossible objects
principles.idea: An alphabet can be a geometric puzzle: reversible, impossible or computable forms that still read.
principles.example: Nedo, Letromaquia exhibition, Museo de Bellas Artes, 1975

keyWorks.title: Gráfica 1 exhibition, Museo de Bellas Artes
Emblem for the Venezuelan pavilion, New York World's Fair

movements.name: Cuban Poster
movements.summary: After 1959 Havana's film institute and solidarity organisation commissioned thousands of silkscreened and offset posters that sold cinema and revolution without selling products.

principles.name: A poster with nothing to sell
principles.idea: With advertising abolished, posters advertised films and causes, so designers could pursue metaphor and wit instead of product benefit.
principles.example: René Azcuy, De la guerra americana, ICAIC, 1969

principles.name: Silkscreen as the house technique
principles.idea: Short runs of hand-pulled screen prints in flat, saturated, overprinted colour made every film poster a small edition and gave the school its look.
principles.example: Alfredo Rostgaard, Hanoi martes 13, screen print signed 'rostgaard/67', 1967

principles.name: One image, every language
principles.idea: Solidarity posters were lettered in Spanish, English, French and Arabic and folded into Tricontinental magazine, so a single image travelled the Global South.
principles.example: Elena Serrano, Day of the Heroic Guerrilla, OSPAAAL, 1968

principles.name: Repetition as rhetoric
principles.idea: A single photographic icon multiplied, scaled or tiled becomes a mass rather than a portrait.
principles.example: Elena Serrano, Che's face repeated in diminishing squares across a red South America, 1968

principles.name: Pop against pop
principles.idea: The visual language of US pop and psychedelia was borrowed and turned against US policy.
principles.example: Alfredo Rostgaard, Black Power poster for OSPAAAL, 1968

keyWorks.title: Día del Guerrillero Heroico (Day of the Heroic Guerrilla), OSPAAAL
Day of World Solidarity with the Cuban Revolution, 26 July

movements.name: Mexico 68
movements.summary: An Olympic identity that fused op-art line with pre-Hispanic pattern and ran from logotype to street paving, then became the Mexico City Metro's pictograms.

principles.name: The logotype generates the system
principles.idea: Radiating parallel lines grown out of the letters of MEXICO68 become a pattern that extends to posters, clothing, stamps and the street.
principles.example: Lance Wyman and Eduardo Terrazas, MEXICO68 logotype and posters, 1968

principles.name: Local form, international code
principles.idea: The concentric-line pattern is widely read as both op art and Wixárika (Huichol) yarn work, so one mark spoke to world media and to Mexicans.
principles.example: Official Mexico 1968 Olympic poster, Eduardo Terrazas and Lance Wyman, 1968

principles.name: Signs for people who cannot read the words
principles.idea: Each station gets a simple pictogram drawn from its name or neighbourhood, coloured by its line, for a city with high illiteracy.
principles.example: Lance Wyman, Mexico City Metro station pictograms, line 1 opened September 1969

principles.name: Urban design as identity
principles.idea: Colour coding painted on pavements, kiosks and signage lets the whole city wear the event, not just the stadiums.
principles.example: Eduardo Terrazas, Olympic urban design programme, 1968

movements.name: Tropicália
movements.summary: Brazil's late-1960s cannibal counterculture: concrete rigour, pop, psychedelia and Northeastern colour mixed on film posters and record covers under dictatorship.

principles.name: Cannibalise everything
principles.idea: Following Oswald de Andrade's 1928 Manifesto Antropófago, foreign and local, high and low are swallowed and recombined rather than chosen between.
principles.example: Tropicália ou Panis et Circencis album, 1968

principles.name: Colour as provocation
principles.idea: Saturated, clashing colour is used as political temperature under military rule, not as decoration.
principles.example: Rogério Duarte, Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol poster, released two months after the 1964 coup

principles.name: Concrete discipline, psychedelic surface
principles.idea: Ulm-literate designers kept structure and type control while letting the surface go lysergic.
principles.example: Rogério Duarte, cover for Gilberto Gil's 1968 album

principles.name: Environment over object
principles.idea: The work is a space you walk through, not a picture you look at.
principles.example: Hélio Oiticica, Tropicália installation, Nova Objetividade Brasileira, MAM Rio, 1967

keyWorks.title: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol poster

movements.name: Chilean Popular Graphics
movements.summary: Record covers, street murals, mass paperbacks and even a cybernetic control room gave Allende's Chile a hopeful, flat-colour, hand-drawn public language until the 1973 coup.

principles.name: The record sleeve as poster
principles.idea: Album covers for the Nueva Canción were the movement's most widely owned images, carrying its politics into homes.
principles.example: Vicente Larrea, cover of Víctor Jara and Quilapayún, Canciones folklóricas de América, 1967

principles.name: Murals by brigade
principles.idea: Fast, collective wall painting with a fixed iconography (wheat ear, fist, star, birds, workers) outlined in black over flat colour.
principles.example: Brigada Ramona Parra with Roberto Matta, El primer gol del pueblo chileno, La Granja, 1971

principles.name: Print for the majority
principles.idea: A state publisher produces cheap books and magazines for mass readership, making editorial design a social service.
principles.example: Editora Nacional Quimantú, founded 1971

principles.name: Design the state's instruments
principles.idea: Ulm-trained designers apply interface and industrial design to national infrastructure.
principles.example: Gui Bonsiepe's team, Project Cybersyn operations room, 1972

keyWorks.title: Canciones folklóricas de América album cover (Vicente Larrea)
El primer gol del pueblo chileno (Brigada Ramona Parra and Roberto Matta)
Project Cybersyn operations room (Gui Bonsiepe's team)

movements.name: Latin American Type Design
movements.summary: A continental type-design scene, from Buenos Aires typographic publishing to digital foundries and a regional biennial, selling Latin American letterforms to the world.

principles.name: A regional canon
principles.idea: A biennial that travels between countries builds a shared Latin American type culture rather than many national ones.
principles.example: Bienal Tipos Latinos, first edition 2004

principles.name: Sell to the world from the periphery
principles.idea: Digital distribution lets a foundry outside the centres reach global brands directly.
principles.example: Latinotype, founded in Concepción, Chile, 2008; Trend among MyFonts' most popular fonts, 2013

principles.name: Signage as a national typeface practice
principles.idea: Large wayfinding commissions become the testing ground for custom lettering.
principles.example: Diseño Shakespear, Buenos Aires Subte signage, 1995-2008

figures.name: Leopoldo Méndez
figures.role: Printmaker, co-founder of the Taller de Gráfica Popular
figures.summary: Mexico's central political printmaker, heir to Posada, who co-founded the TGP in 1937 and later cut prints for Mexican cinema.

principles.name: Anonymity in the service of the message
principles.idea: He kept individual credit small and worked through collectives, treating authorship as less important than reach.
principles.example: Collaborative TGP broadsides, from 1937

principles.name: The print as cinema
principles.idea: Sequences of prints work like film stills, and prints can enter film itself.
principles.example: Engravings for Emilio Fernández's Río Escondido, late 1940s

principles.name: Posada's line, modern politics
principles.idea: The popular broadside's directness is used for anti-fascism and labour, not just satire.
principles.example: En el nombre de Cristo, 1942

keyWorks.title: Illustrations for Incidentes melódicos del mundo irracional
Engraved mural dedicated to José Guadalupe Posada, Talleres Gráficos de la Nación

figures.name: Tomás Maldonado
figures.summary: Buenos Aires concrete painter who co-founded Arte Concreto-Invención, edited Nueva Visión, then shaped the Ulm model as teacher and rector.

principles.name: Design as science-informed method
principles.idea: Design should balance science and making, using planning methods, perception theory and semiotics rather than artistic intuition.
principles.example: Ulm, Science and Design, 1964

principles.name: Systems over objects
principles.idea: Codes and systems for a company matter more than any single beautiful artefact.
principles.example: Sign and code systems for Olivetti and La Rinascente with Gui Bonsiepe, 1964-1967

principles.name: Design as environmental responsibility
principles.idea: Design has to answer to ecology and society, not only to industry.
principles.example: La speranza progettuale, 1970 (English: Design, Nature, and Revolution, 1972)

figures.name: Juan Carlos Distéfano
figures.summary: Organised the Instituto Di Tella's graphic design department in the 1960s, Argentina's first professional design studio, then became a major figurative sculptor.

principles.name: A horizontal studio
principles.idea: He described the Di Tella team as having no rigid line between those who direct and those who execute.
principles.example: Departamento de Diseño Gráfico, Instituto Di Tella, 1963-1970

principles.name: Swiss structure, New York wit
principles.idea: Swiss order is combined with the idea-led advertising of the New York School inside one institutional voice.
principles.example: Di Tella exhibition posters and catalogues, 1960s

principles.name: Make it by hand, fast and cheap
principles.idea: Small budgets and short deadlines are worked with directly, not hidden.
principles.example: Di Tella programmes and flyers, 1960s

keyWorks.title: Prize-winning poster for the Siam Di Tella fiftieth anniversary competition

figures.name: Rubén Fontana
figures.summary: Di Tella designer who ran its department in 1969-70, then built Argentine typographic culture through tipoGráfica magazine and the Fontana ND typeface.

principles.name: Typography is culture, not styling
principles.idea: A magazine and a school can make typography a shared intellectual discipline for a region.
principles.example: tipoGráfica (tpG) magazine, Buenos Aires, from 1987

principles.name: A Latin American text face
principles.idea: Text typefaces can be designed from the region for international distribution.
principles.example: Fontana ND, published by Neufville Digital

keyWorks.title: Co-direction of the Di Tella graphic design department

figures.name: Guillermo González Ruiz
figures.summary: Architect-designer who led the 1971-72 Buenos Aires signage plan with Ronald Shakespear and directed graphic design at the University of Buenos Aires.

principles.name: Signage is architecture
principles.idea: Wayfinding is designed with an architect's sense of space, sightlines and urban scale.
principles.example: Plan Visual de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, 1971-1972

principles.name: Teach the profession into existence
principles.idea: A public university programme is the way to make design a recognised discipline in a country.
principles.example: Director of Graphic Design at FADU, Universidad de Buenos Aires, 1985-1990

keyWorks.title: Plan Visual de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires (with Ronald Shakespear)

figures.name: Ronald Shakespear
figures.role: Graphic designer, wayfinding and identity designer
figures.summary: Rosario-born designer of Buenos Aires's urban signage, hospital system and Subte wayfinding, and more than a thousand identities.

principles.name: The city as a client
principles.idea: Wayfinding at city scale, for streets, hospitals and subway, is the most public form of graphic design.
principles.example: Municipal hospitals signage, with Raúl Shakespear, 1978

principles.name: A family studio across generations
principles.idea: A practice carries a consistent system language across decades by passing projects to the next generation.
principles.example: Subte signage with Lorenzo and Juan Shakespear, 1995-2008

keyWorks.title: Plan Visual de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires (with Guillermo González Ruiz)

figures.name: Geraldo de Barros
figures.role: Photographer, painter, graphic and furniture designer
figures.summary: Abstract photographer and Ruptura founder who moved concrete art into industry: Unilabor furniture, the Forminform design office and mass-produced modern objects.

principles.name: Cut the negative
principles.idea: Photographs are constructed by scratching, masking and multiple exposure, so the camera produces form rather than records it.
principles.example: Fotoformas, MASP, 1950

principles.name: Art for the masses through production
principles.idea: Modern design reaches people through cooperatives and factories, not galleries.
principles.example: Unilabor furniture cooperative, 1954-1967

principles.name: The right to error
principles.idea: He treated mistakes as part of the method; error is how new form appears.
principles.example: Sobras, his last photographs, made with Ana Moraes, from 1996

keyWorks.title: IV Centenário de São Paulo festival posters (with Alexandre Wollner)

figures.name: Décio Pignatari
figures.summary: Noigandres poet whose 'beba coca cola' turned a slogan into an anti-advertisement, and who taught information theory and semiotics to Brazilian designers.

principles.name: Detourn the slogan
principles.idea: The grammar of advertising, short words and repetition, is rearranged until it critiques itself.
principles.example: beba coca cola, 1957

principles.name: Information before ornament
principles.idea: Communication theory, how much a sign carries, is a design tool.
principles.example: Informação, Linguagem, Comunicação, 1968

keyWorks.title: Teoria da Poesia Concreta (with the Campos brothers)

figures.name: Haroldo de Campos
figures.summary: Noigandres co-founder and theorist whose idea of translation as creative re-making ('transcreation') gave concrete poetry its intellectual reach.

principles.name: Transcreation
principles.idea: Translation re-creates form as well as meaning, so the visual and sonic structure of a text is what gets carried over.
principles.example: His translations collected alongside the concrete theory of Teoria da Poesia Concreta, 1965

principles.name: Structure over line
principles.idea: The poem's spatial structure, not the verse line, is the unit of composition.
principles.example: Plano-piloto para poesia concreta, 1958

keyWorks.title: Teoria da Poesia Concreta (with Augusto de Campos and Décio Pignatari)

figures.name: Augusto de Campos
figures.summary: Noigandres poet whose colour-coded Poetamenos (1955) launched Brazilian concrete poetry, and who carried the method into poster-poems, objects and digital media.

principles.name: Colour as voice
principles.idea: Each colour in a poem marks a different voice or timbre, like a score.
principles.example: Poetamenos, Noigandres 2, 1955

principles.name: The poem as poster
principles.idea: Political poems are printed as large-format posters made from found commercial type.
principles.example: Popcretos series, 1964-1966

principles.name: The reader assembles it
principles.idea: Pop-up and folding structures make reading physical and interactive.
principles.example: Poemóbiles, with Julio Plaza, 1974

figures.name: Alexandre Wollner
figures.summary: Ulm-trained 'father of Brazilian modern design', co-founder of Forminform and ESDI, whose constructed marks defined Brazilian corporate identity.

principles.name: Construct the mark
principles.idea: Symbols are built from simple geometric parts (semicircles, triangles, lozenges) so they can be redrawn, scaled and remembered.
principles.example: Sardinhas Coqueiro mark and packaging, Forminform, 1958

principles.name: Research before form
principles.idea: Identity starts from historical and functional research, so form and colour are argued from the client's history rather than chosen for mood.
principles.example: Banco Itaú mark, adopted 1973, later recoloured orange by DPZ's Francesc Petit, a change criticised for ignoring the original research

principles.name: Concrete art as a design grammar
principles.idea: The concrete painter's training in proportion and the module carries straight into identity work.
principles.example: Cinemateca Brasileira logotype, 1954

keyWorks.title: Cinemateca Brasileira logotype (for the MAM Filmoteca)

figures.name: Aloísio Magalhães
figures.summary: Recife-born designer of Brazil's banknotes, the first Globo symbol and the Rio IV Centenário mark, who co-founded ESDI and later ran national heritage policy.

principles.name: Design for a nation's identity
principles.idea: Currency, anniversaries and broadcasters are where a country meets its own image daily.
principles.example: Cruzeiro novo banknote competition, won 1966

principles.name: Pattern as security and beauty
principles.idea: Moiré and mirrored designs make a note both hard to forge and readable whichever way it is held.
principles.example: 1,000-cruzeiro 'Barão' note with mirrored design, 1978

principles.name: Heritage is design's raw material
principles.idea: Vernacular craft and cultural memory are the resources a modern design culture builds from.
principles.example: Centro Nacional de Referência Cultural, from 1975

keyWorks.title: IV Centenário do Rio de Janeiro symbol

figures.name: Rogério Duarte
figures.summary: Tropicália's graphic designer: Cinema Novo posters and the 1968 Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil covers, mixing Ulm-taught structure with psychedelic colour.

principles.name: Colour researched, then released
principles.idea: Colour is a researched instrument; he described the Deus e o Diabo poster as a new conception of colour born of deep research.
principles.example: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol poster, 1964

principles.name: Know the rules to break them
principles.idea: Grounding in Ulm-style rational design is what lets the pop and psychedelic break land.
principles.example: Gilberto Gil album cover, 1968

principles.name: Design for the left without its clichés
principles.idea: Political graphics need not look like socialist realism; vernacular and pop sources can carry politics.
principles.example: Head of visual arts at the Centro Popular de Cultura (UNE), early 1960s

keyWorks.title: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol poster

figures.name: Gerd Leufert
figures.summary: German-trained émigré who made El Farol and the Museo de Bellas Artes into laboratories, and staged Venezuela's first graphic design exhibition in 1961.

principles.name: The client publication as experiment
principles.idea: An oil company's magazine is used to test a new graphic language, free of folkloric illustration.
principles.example: El Farol redesign, 1957-1959

principles.name: The museum as client and stage
principles.idea: Museum catalogues and exhibitions both practise and present design.
principles.example: Gráfica 1, Museo de Bellas Artes, Caracas, 1961

keyWorks.title: Venezuelan pavilion emblem, New York World's Fair

figures.name: Nedo Mion Ferrario
figures.summary: Milan-born Caracas designer, known as Nedo, who art-directed El Farol for thirteen years and drew around sixty geometric, 'impossible' and reversible alphabets.

principles.name: The total magazine
principles.idea: Paper changes, flaps, cover-to-body flow and halftone experiments make the turning of the page itself the design.
principles.example: El Farol, sixty consecutive issues, 1959-1972

principles.name: Impossible letters
principles.idea: Alphabets built on optical paradox (impossible, reversible, computable) are still legible type.
principles.example: Reversibles exhibition, Museo de Bellas Artes, 1969

principles.name: Teach for decades
principles.idea: A design chair held for 27 years forms a national profession.
principles.example: Design chair at the Escuela de Artes Plásticas Cristóbal Rojas, from 1959

figures.name: Eduardo Muñoz Bachs
figures.summary: Self-taught Valencia-born designer of ICAIC's first poster in 1960 and over 2,000 film posters, with a childlike drawn figure and hand lettering.

principles.name: Draw like a child, think like an adult
principles.idea: A naive, comic drawing style and hand-made lettering carry sophisticated irony.
principles.example: La trampa poster, ICAIC, 1967

principles.name: The figure is the poster
principles.idea: The human face or whole body dominates; colours are bright but never shocking.
principles.example: En busca de un hombre poster, ICAIC, 1967

principles.name: Volume as a style
principles.idea: Thousands of posters over a lifetime make a recognisable personal language within an institution.
principles.example: No hay regreso para Johnny poster, ICAIC, 1971

figures.name: Raúl Martínez
figures.summary: Former Los Once abstractionist who became Cuba's pop portraitist of Martí and Camilo Cienfuegos and a designer for ICAIC, Casa de las Américas and OSPAAAL.

principles.name: The hero, multiplied
principles.idea: Portraits of national heroes are repeated in grids of flat colour, pop serialisation turned into revolutionary iconography.
principles.example: Pop portraits of José Martí, mid-1960s

principles.name: Painter and designer as one practice
principles.idea: The same artist moves between painting, book design and posters without a hierarchy.
principles.example: Day of World Solidarity with the Cuban Revolution poster, OSPAAAL, 1968

keyWorks.title: Day of World Solidarity with the Cuban Revolution, 26 July
Lucía film poster (for Humberto Solás's 1968 film)

figures.name: Félix Beltrán
figures.summary: New York-trained Cuban designer who led the government's Comisión de Orientación Revolucionaria posters, taught design from 1963 and moved to Mexico in 1982.

principles.name: Simplicity as effectiveness
principles.idea: One idea, minimum elements: simplicity is the basis of communication that works.
principles.example: Vietnam will win poster, 1968

principles.name: Theory alongside practice
principles.idea: A designer writes and publishes on design to build the discipline.
principles.example: Desde el diseño, Havana, 1970; Letragrafía, 1973; Acerca del diseño, 1975

principles.name: The archive as infrastructure
principles.idea: Collecting design builds the discipline's memory.
principles.example: First international graphic design archive in Latin America, Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana, Mexico City

figures.name: René Azcuy
figures.summary: ICAIC's most austere film-poster designer: black, white and one colour, a single cropped photographic image, and a metaphor instead of a scene.

principles.name: One image, one idea
principles.idea: A single high-contrast photographic fragment stands in for the whole film.
principles.example: De la guerra americana, ICAIC, 1969

principles.name: Restraint as intensity
principles.idea: Minimal palette and large empty space make violence or desire more charged than illustration would.
principles.example: Sin esperanza, ICAIC, 1967

figures.name: Alfredo Rostgaard
figures.summary: Guantánamo-born caricaturist who became OSPAAAL's art director in 1966, mixing pop, psychedelia and humour into the most travelled solidarity posters.

principles.name: Humour for serious subjects
principles.idea: Caricature and playfulness make grave political subjects memorable rather than solemn.
principles.example: Create two, three... many Vietnams, 1967

principles.name: Borrow the enemy's pop
principles.idea: Warhol-like commercial graphics and psychedelic line are turned to anti-imperialist ends.
principles.example: Black Power poster, OSPAAAL, 1968

principles.name: Silkscreen colour as structure
principles.idea: Flat overprinted inks carry the composition, not just fill it.
principles.example: Hanoi martes 13, colour screen print, 1967

figures.name: Lance Wyman
figures.summary: New Jersey designer who developed the MEXICO68 logotype and its applications, then the Mexico City Metro pictograms and the Washington Metro map.

principles.name: A logo should become a programme
principles.idea: A mark that adapts to signs and environments can drive an entire design programme.
principles.example: Chrysler pavilion pointing-hand logo and signs, New York World's Fair, 1964

principles.name: Functional aesthetic
principles.idea: He credits the no-nonsense functional aesthetic of the sea and the factories he grew up around as a key influence.
principles.example: Mexico City Metro station pictograms, 1969

principles.name: Clarity over geography
principles.idea: A transit map shows routes, transfers and landmarks clearly rather than distances to scale.
principles.example: Washington Metro map, mid-1970s, revised by Wyman in 2012

figures.name: Eduardo Terrazas
figures.summary: Architect who coordinated the Mexico 68 identity programme and its urban design under Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, then became a painter of systematic geometric series.

principles.name: Identity at city scale
principles.idea: An event's identity is applied to streets, kiosks and pavements so the whole city becomes the medium.
principles.example: Mexico 68 urban design programme, 1968

principles.name: Assemble an international team
principles.idea: Local direction plus recruited international designers produce a system neither would alone.
principles.example: Recruiting Lance Wyman and others to the Olympic identity programme, 1966-1968

keyWorks.title: Mexico pavilion, New York World's Fair (with Pedro Ramírez Vázquez)
Mexico 68 identity and urban design programme

events.label: Taller de Gráfica Popular founded
events.note: Leopoldo Méndez, Pablo O'Higgins and Luis Arenal found the Mexico City print collective, making the linocut a mass political medium.

events.label: First Bienal de São Paulo
events.note: Max Bill's prize and his MASP retrospective the same year ignite Brazilian concrete art and, through it, Brazilian modern design.

events.label: Cuban Revolution
events.note: ICAIC is founded in March 1959, and with advertising gone the poster becomes a cultural rather than commercial medium.

events.label: Brasília inaugurated
events.note: Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer's capital, opened 21 April 1960, makes modernism Brazil's official national image.

events.label: ESDI opens in Rio de Janeiro
events.note: Latin America's first university-level design school, built on the Ulm model with Wollner, Magalhães and Bergmiller among its founders.

events.label: Tricontinental Conference, Havana
events.note: Founds OSPAAAL, whose multilingual solidarity posters, folded into Tricontinental magazine, become a graphic network for the Global South.

events.label: Mexico 68 Olympics and Tlatelolco
events.note: The most complete Olympic identity yet opens days after the 2 October massacre; protesters answer with a bayonet-pierced dove.

events.label: Mexico City Metro opens
events.note: Line 1 opens on 4-5 September 1969 with Lance Wyman's station pictograms, a wayfinding system designed for every literacy level.

events.label: Instituto Di Tella closes its art centres
events.note: Under the Onganía regime the Buenos Aires avant-garde's home, and Argentina's first professional design department, close in 1970.

events.label: Chilean coup
events.note: The 11 September coup ends Allende's government, painting over Unidad Popular murals and scattering its designers into exile.

events.label: First Bienal Tipos Latinos
events.note: A travelling Latin American type biennial gives the region's type designers a shared stage.
